children: U.S. and European government bond yields fell in early European trade, pulling away from multiyear highs following a decline in oil prices and signals from a Federal Reserve official that there isn't an urgent need to raise interest rates.

New York Fed President John Williams told CNBC in an interview on Wednesday that "there's no clear signs right now...whether monetary policy currently is sufficient to make sure we bring inflation back to target in the next year or two, or whether we need to see further action to do that."
His comments prompted a reversal in yield rises which continued overnight and into European trading.
The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield last traded 2.8 basis points lower at 4.765%, having risen to 4.818% on Wednesday, the highest since November 2023, according to Tradeweb.

In Europe, the 10-year German Bund yield fell 1.5 basis points to 3.363%, after hitting a 15-year high of 3.395% on Wednesday. The 10-year U.K. gilt yield declined 4.1 basis points to 5.198%, down from Wednesday's 19-year peak of 5.294%.

U.S. money markets now price a 59% probability of a rate hike this month, down from nearly 70% on Wednesday, LSEG data showed. Weak U.S. ADP private payrolls figures on Wednesday contributed to bringing down rate-hike expectations as investors await Friday's key monthly nonfarm payrolls data.
Declining oil prices were another boost for bonds, with the price of Brent crude oil down 1.2% at $94.52.
However, the selloff in bonds might not be over.

Bond yields have more room to rise due to multiple unresolved issues, conflicts, and no clear resolution timeline anywhere, Natalia Lojevsky, managing director at ​CIFC Asset Management, said in a note.
"You have two stresses hitting bond markets around the globe at the same time: a structural supply problem from deficits and massive issuance rates of corporate and sovereign​," she said.
That combination explains the recent jump in yields and why it has been relatively aggressive, she said.
Friday's release of U.S. employment data will be a key input into market expectations of the Fed's decision at the Sept. 16 meeting.

"When we triangulate across all the labor market data that will be released this week, we're expecting that the labor market will be room temperature, rather than boiling or frozen. And that would be good news for the Fed," Russell Investments' senior investment strategist BeiChen Lin said in a note.

However, if job creation were to come in significantly stronger than consensus expectations, "that might cause the Fed to give more consideration to rate hikes if inflation does not cooperate," he said.
Analysts in The Wall Street Journal's poll forecast the data to show 53,000 jobs were created in August.
